title: OpenAI slashes GPT-5.6 Luna prices by 80 percent, three weeks after launch
subtitle: OpenAI cut the cheapest GPT-5.6 tier from $1/$6 to $0.20/$1.20 per million input/output tokens, undercutting DeepSeek and putting frontier-lab pricing power under visible strain.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI cut the API prices of the two lower-cost models in its GPT-5.6 family on July 30. Luna, the budget tier, dropped 80 percent to $0.20 per million input tokens and $1.20 per million output tokens — down from $1 and $6. Terra, the mid-tier, dropped 20 percent to $2 input and $12 output. The flagship Sol model was left unchanged at $5 and $30. The cut arrived only 21 days after the GPT-5.6 family launched on July 9, meaning the initial price sheet did not survive a single billing cycle.

The mechanism worth understanding is that the pressure is not coming from Anthropic or Google. It is coming from Chinese open-weight models. A CNBC investigation on July 7 showed that Chinese models — DeepSeek V4, Qwen, Kimi K3 — had captured roughly 46 percent of US enterprise token usage on OpenRouter, at times peaking above US-origin models. At the previous $1 input rate, Luna was simply not competitive per token with DeepSeek. At $0.20, it is cheaper than DeepSeek on input while remaining more expensive on output — a positioning choice that assumes enterprise workloads are input-heavy retrieval, not output-heavy generation.

In context, this is the third major frontier-lab price cut of 2026 (after Anthropic's Opus 5 half-price launch on July 26 and Google's Gemini 3.5 Flash tier repricing in May), and the pattern is consistent: the very top of the market — Sol, Opus 5, Gemini 3.6 Pro — is holding price, while everything beneath it is racing toward the marginal cost of inference. That is what a commoditized layer looks like forming underneath a still-differentiated frontier. For anyone tracking whether AI is a monopoly business or a utility one, the shape of this year's pricing curve is the answer.

For learners: if you are building on the API, the practical read is that any workload you were running on Luna at the July 9 price is now 80 percent cheaper — check your bill. And if you were choosing between Luna and DeepSeek on cost alone, the calculation you did three weeks ago is now wrong. Recheck price sheets before you commit to a stack; the useful mental model for 2026 is that inference cost halves roughly every four to six months at the mid-tier.
